title: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST
directAnswer: The whole problem is one BST insight: an in-order traversal visits nodes in sorted ascending order, and in a sorted sequence the minimum gap must be between two ADJACENT values. So do an in-order DFS, keep a single `prev` pointer to the previously visited value, and at each node update the answer with `node.val − prev`. No need to collect all values — just track the previous one and the running minimum.

remember.pattern: In-order traversal (sorted order) + track previous value for adjacent gap
remember.formula:
prev = null, best = +inf
inorder(node):
    if node is null: return
    inorder(node.left)
    if prev != null: best = min(best, node.val - prev)
    prev = node.val
    inorder(node.right)
rules: **In-order** traversal of a BST yields values in **sorted ascending** order — this is THE property you exploit.
In a sorted sequence the smallest difference is always between **adjacent** elements, never far-apart ones.
Track a single `prev` value; compare `node.val − prev` — values are increasing so the gap is non-negative.
Initialize `prev` to a sentinel (null/None) and only compare once a real previous value exists.
No need to store all values — **O(1)** extra state (prev + best) beyond the recursion stack suffices.
whenToUse: Find a min/closeness statistic over BST values where sorted order helps
Anything reducible to 'compare adjacent elements in sorted order'
You can traverse in-order instead of materializing and sorting an array
Streaming the sorted sequence with O(1) memory between elements
antiSignals: It's NOT a BST (arbitrary tree) → in-order isn't sorted; collect and sort, or use a different idea
You need the actual pair, not just the gap → still works, just remember which two
Need pairwise difference across non-adjacent constraints → may need all values
Looking for a target sum/closest value to a query → BST search, not adjacent-gap scan
remember.takeaway: Minimum Absolute Difference in BST is a one-line insight wrapped in a traversal: in-order on a BST is sorted, and sorted means the answer lives between neighbors. Carrying a single `prev` pointer turns it into an O(1)-space scan and is the template for every 'adjacent in sorted order' BST problem.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you connect 'BST + minimum difference' to 'in-order traversal gives sorted order, so compare adjacent values', rather than brute-forcing all pairs or sorting a collected array.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Comparing every pair of nodes O(n²), or computing differences between a node and its parent/children (not the in-order neighbor), which misses the true minimum gap.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the two-part insight crisply — in-order is sorted, min gap is between adjacents — and implement it with a single prev pointer in O(1) extra space, then mention the iterative-stack variant for the no-recursion follow-up.

problemStatement:
Given the `root` of a Binary Search Tree (BST), return the **minimum absolute difference between the values of any two different nodes** in the tree.

Note: This is the same as LeetCode 783, *Minimum Distance Between BST Nodes*.
constraints: The number of nodes is in the range [2, 10⁴]
The tree is guaranteed to be a valid BST
understanding: We want the smallest gap between any two node values in the tree. The naive reading invites comparing all pairs, but the BST guarantee changes everything: an in-order traversal emits the values already sorted. In any sorted list, the minimum difference is necessarily between two consecutive entries — so we only ever compare each value with the one visited just before it.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the tree guaranteed to be a BST?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes. That's the crux — in-order traversal of a BST produces sorted values, which is what lets us look only at adjacent pairs.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Why is the answer always between adjacent in-order values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In a sorted sequence, any non-adjacent pair has at least one element between them, so their difference is ≥ the difference of a tighter adjacent pair. The minimum must be a neighbor gap.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can node values repeat?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: In a strict BST values are distinct; if duplicates were allowed the minimum difference could be 0. The adjacent-comparison handles either case correctly.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do I need O(n) space to store the sorted values?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: No. Tracking a single previous value plus the running minimum is O(1) extra space beyond the recursion stack.

diagrams.title: Why only adjacent in-order pairs matter
diagrams.caption: In-order on a BST sorts the values; the smallest gap in a sorted line is always between neighbors.

approaches.name: In-Order DFS Tracking the Previous Value (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: Lead with this. Frame it as 'in-order gives sorted order, so the minimum gap is between consecutive values — carry a prev pointer'.
hints: It's a BST. Is there a traversal order that visits the values from smallest to largest?
In-order traversal of a BST yields sorted values. In a sorted list, where can the minimum difference possibly be?
Only between adjacent elements. So traverse in-order, remember the previously visited value, and at each node take min(best, node.val − prev).
approaches.complexityReasoning: A single in-order traversal visits each node once with O(1) work → O(n) time. Extra state is just prev and best (O(1)); the recursion stack costs O(h) → O(log n) balanced, O(n) degenerate.
approaches.explanation:
This problem is a litmus test for whether you internalize the single most useful BST fact: **an in-order traversal (left, node, right) of a binary search tree visits the values in strictly ascending order**. Once you see that, the problem nearly solves itself.

**Why sorted order collapses the search.** The brute-force reading — 'minimum difference between *any* two nodes' — sounds like it requires examining all `O(n²)` pairs. But once the values are sorted, a classic fact applies: **the minimum absolute difference in a sorted sequence is always between two adjacent elements**. Intuitively, if two values are not adjacent, there's at least one value sitting between them, and that in-between value is closer to each of them than they are to each other. So any non-adjacent pair can be beaten by an adjacent one, and we only ever need to compare neighbors.

**Why a single `prev` pointer suffices.** We don't need to materialize the sorted array at all. As the in-order traversal unfolds, it produces the values one at a time in increasing order. If we remember just the *previous* value emitted, then at each new node we can compute `node.val − prev` — the gap to its immediate predecessor in sorted order — and fold it into a running minimum `best`. After the whole traversal, `best` holds the global minimum. State is `O(1)` beyond the call stack: one previous value and one best-so-far.

**Why the subtraction needs no absolute value.** Because in-order yields ascending values, `node.val` is always ≥ `prev`, so `node.val − prev` is already non-negative — it *is* the absolute difference. We still guard the very first node: there's no predecessor yet, so we initialize `prev` to a sentinel (null/None) and skip the comparison until a real previous value exists. Forgetting that guard either crashes on a null `prev` or pollutes `best` with a bogus comparison against zero.

**Why in-order specifically, not pre/post-order.** Pre-order and post-order do *not* emit BST values in sorted order, so the adjacent-gap argument wouldn't hold for them. The left-node-right sequencing is precisely what aligns the traversal with the sorted order, which is the linchpin of the whole approach. This same template — in-order plus a `prev` pointer — also detects whether a tree is a valid BST (check `prev < node.val`) and finds the k-th smallest element, so it's worth committing to muscle memory.
approaches.insight: Two facts compose into the answer: (1) in-order on a BST is sorted, and (2) the tightest gap in a sorted list is between neighbors. Combine them and an apparently O(n²) pairwise problem becomes a single O(n) pass with O(1) extra memory. The `prev`-pointer in-order scan is the BST Swiss-army knife.

Skip the very first node, which has no in-order predecessor to compare against.
Ascending order means node.val ≥ prev, so the difference is the absolute gap to the predecessor.
Current value becomes prev for the next (larger) node — the heart of the scan.
Then the right subtree, whose values are larger, continuing the sorted order.

Only compare once a real previous value has been seen.
Adjacent gap in sorted order; non-negative because values ascend.
Record this value as the predecessor of the next node.
Right subtree last — larger values keep the order sorted.

pitfalls: Using pre-order or post-order, which don't emit sorted values.
Comparing a node only to its parent/children instead of its in-order neighbor.
Forgetting the null-prev guard on the first node.
Collecting all values into a list and sorting — correct but wastes O(n) space and the BST property.

approaches.name: Iterative In-Order with an Explicit Stack
approaches.whenToMention: Offer for the 'no recursion' follow-up or to avoid stack overflow on a degenerate BST. Same logic, explicit stack.
hints: Recursion's call stack is what produces the in-order sequence. To go iterative, simulate that stack yourself.
Push left children until null, then pop a node (that's the next in sorted order), process it, and move to its right child.
Keep the same prev pointer and best minimum; compare each popped node's value to prev.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Each node is pushed and popped exactly once → O(n) time. The stack holds at most one root-to-leftmost path → O(h) space, matching the recursion.
approaches.explanation:
When the interviewer asks for a non-recursive version, or when a degenerate (linked-list-shaped) BST threatens a stack overflow, we make the in-order traversal explicit with our own stack — while keeping the `prev`/`best` logic byte-for-byte identical.

**Why the stack reproduces in-order.** In-order means 'fully explore the left spine before visiting a node, then go right'. The iterative idiom captures this with two moves: from the current node, push it and walk left until there's no left child (stacking the entire left spine); then pop — the popped node is the smallest unvisited value, i.e. the next in sorted order — process it, and set the current pointer to its right child to repeat. This push-left-then-pop-then-go-right dance emits exactly the same ascending sequence the recursion would.

**Why the comparison logic is unchanged.** Each time we pop a node we have the next sorted value. We compare it to `prev` exactly as before — `best = min(best, node.val − prev)` when `prev` exists — and then set `prev` to this value. The algorithmic content is identical; only the mechanism that orders the visits has moved from the language runtime's call stack into our explicit one.

**Why this guards against deep trees.** A BST can degenerate into a chain of `n` nodes (e.g., values inserted in sorted order), giving a height of `n`. Recursion would then recurse `n` deep and risk a stack overflow in languages with limited stack depth. The iterative version uses heap-allocated stack storage, which typically tolerates much larger depths, so it's the safer choice when `n` is large and the tree might be skewed.

**Why the complexity is the same.** Every node is pushed once and popped once, so time is `O(n)`. The explicit stack holds at most one root-to-leftmost-leaf path at a time, so its peak size is the height `h` — identical `O(h)` space to the recursion, just relocated. There's no asymptotic difference, only the practical robustness of not relying on the call stack.
approaches.insight: The recursion's implicit call stack and this explicit stack produce the very same in-order sequence; swapping one for the other changes nothing about the prev-pointer logic. Recognizing 'in-order = push the left spine, pop, go right' lets you de-recurse any in-order BST algorithm on demand.

dryRun.intro: Explicit stack yields in-order 0,1,12,48,49. prev tracks the previous popped value.

steps.action: prev null → no compare; prev=0; go right (none)
1 − 0 = 1 → best=1; prev=1; go right to 48, push left spine 48,12

code.python:
def getMinimumDifference(self, root: TreeNode) -> int:
    stack = []
    cur = root
    prev = None
    best = float('inf')
    while cur is not None or stack:
        while cur is not None:          # push the entire left spine
            stack.append(cur)
            cur = cur.left
        cur = stack.pop()               # next value in sorted order
        if prev is not None:
            best = min(best, cur.val - prev)
        prev = cur.val
        cur = cur.right                 # then explore the right subtree
    return best

java.explanation: Walk and stack the whole left spine so the smallest unvisited value sits on top.
Popping gives the next node in ascending order — the in-order successor.
Compare to the previous popped value: the adjacent gap in sorted order.
After visiting a node, move to its right subtree to continue in-order.

python.explanation: Push the left spine; deepest-left is the smallest value.
Next sorted value emerges from the stack.
Update the running minimum with the neighbor gap.
Proceed to the right subtree, preserving ascending order.

edgeCases.behavior: Left spines are length 1; stack stays shallow, traversal still ascending.
Explicit stack avoids recursion-depth overflow; O(h) heap stack handles it.

pitfalls: Forgetting to push the left spine before popping, breaking sorted order.
Not moving to cur.right after popping, skipping right subtrees.
Comparing with absolute value unnecessarily — values already ascend.

commonMistakes: Brute-forcing all O(n²) pairs instead of using in-order sorted order.
Using pre-order or post-order, which don't yield sorted values.
Comparing a node only to its parent/children rather than its in-order neighbor.
Collecting and sorting values into an array, wasting the BST property and O(n) space.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Comparing all pairs instead of adjacent in-order values
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Checking every pair is O(n²) and ignores the BST structure. The minimum gap is guaranteed to be between consecutive in-order values, so an O(n) scan suffices.

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Wrong traversal order
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Only in-order emits BST values sorted. Using pre-order means node.val − prev is not an adjacent-in-sorted-order gap, so the computed minimum can be wrong.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
def preorder(node):       # WRONG order for a BST
    if node is None:
        return
    if self.prev is not None:
        self.best = min(self.best, abs(node.val - self.prev))
    self.prev = node.val
    preorder(node.left)
    preorder(node.right)

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Missing the first-node guard
commonMistakesDetailed.why: On the very first in-order node there is no predecessor. Comparing against an uninitialized prev (0 or null) either crashes or wrongly seeds best with node.val − 0.
